analogy.body: Saying me: every object can talk about itself

scenes.onScreen: chain.cpp: each function returns the object, so calls chain
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 8] Add returns a reference to a Counter. [HL 9] It adds n to the count. [HL 10] This is a pointer to the current object. Star this is the object itself. [HL 17] Because add returns the object, we can call add again on the result. [HL 18] Two plus three plus ten gives fifteen.

scenes.onScreen: the pointer this points at the object c
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Inside add, the hidden pointer this holds the address of c. That is how add knows which count to change. Each object has its own address, so each call changes the right object.

scenes.onScreen: constfunc.cpp: show promises not to change the object
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 8] This function changes the object, so it is not const. [HL 9] The word const after the brackets is a promise. This function does not change the object. [HL 13] Here the object is const. [HL 14] A const object may only call const functions. Get is const, so the call is fine.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as constfunc dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints seven.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. This is a pointer to the current object. Two. Return star this to chain calls. Three. Const after the brackets is a promise not to change the object. Four. A const object can only call const functions. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: This is a pointer to the current object.
Return star this to chain calls.
Const after the brackets is a promise not to change the object.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A non-const call on a const object
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The object is const, but we call increment. The compiler says passing const Counter as this argument discards qualifiers. That sounds hard, but it means this. A const object cannot call a function that may change it.

scenes.onScreen: The object looked in the mirror and said, I like this.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: The object looked in the mirror and said, I like this.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: mark the right functions const
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a class with a private value. Add three functions: set, get and print. Mark every function that does not change the object as const. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

constfunc.cpp: In function 'int main()':
constfunc.cpp:14:16: error: passing 'const Counter' as 'this' argument discards qualifiers [-fpermissive]
   14 |     c.increment();
      |     ~~~~~~~~~~~^~
constfunc.cpp:8:10: note:   in call to 'void Counter::increment()'
    8 |     void increment() { count_++; }
bug.why: A const object may not change, so it may not call a function that can change it. Remove const from the object, or do not call that function.

pun: "The object looked in the mirror and said, I like this."
challenge: Write a class with a private value. Add three functions: set, get and print. Mark every function that does not change the object as const.
challengeAnswer: Get and print do not change the object, so mark both const. Set changes the value, so it stays non-const.
